old: "Use direct speech to reproduce exact words and indirect speech to report what someone said without quoting the exact words."
new: "You know reported speech from B1 Unit 25 (*estilo indirecto*): after a past reporting verb, the verb moves back one step. This lesson contrasts the two ways of telling what someone said: direct speech repeats the exact words, and indirect speech reports them with *que* and without quotation marks."

old: "Unlike English, which can drop 'that' — 'She said she was tired' — Spanish indirect speech always keeps *que*: dijo *que* *estaba* cansada."
new: "English can drop “that” (“She said she was tired”), but Spanish always keeps *que*: *Ella dijo que estaba cansada*."

old: "Use decir *que*, contar que, explicar que and similar reporting verbs to introduce reported statements."
new: "You know reported statements from B1 Unit 25 (*estilo indirecto*) and the *pluscuamperfecto* from B1 Unit 1. This lesson adds more reporting verbs, *contar*, *explicar*, *informar* and *asegurar*, each followed by *que* and a verb that has moved back one step."

old: "The reporting verb carries its own flavour: *afirmar* sounds more formal and definite than plain *decir*, so choosing it, as in the last example, tells the listener something about how firmly the statement was made."
new: "The reporting verb adds a flavour: *afirmar* and *asegurar* sound firmer and more formal than plain *decir*, as in *La mujer afirmó que había oído un ruido extraño*."

old: "Use preguntar si for yes/no questions and question words for reported information questions."
new: "You know reported questions with *preguntó* and a question word from A2 Unit 14 (*preguntas indirectas*), and *preguntó si* from B1 Unit 53. Use *preguntar si* for a yes/no question and a question word for an information question; the verb moves back one step, as in any report."

old: "A reported question keeps statement word order — me *preguntó* *dónde* *vivía*, not dónde vivía yo — and drops the question marks entirely, since it isn't really a question any more."
new: "A reported question has no question marks, but the question word keeps its accent (*dónde*, *qué*, *quién*), while *si* for a yes/no question has none: *Me preguntó si tenía tiempo*."

old: "When reporting a past conversation, adjust tense, pronouns and time or place expressions when the perspective requires it."
new: "You know from B1 Unit 25 that the verb moves back one step after a past reporting verb, and you met *al día siguiente* there. When you retell a conversation from another place or time, the pronouns and the time and place words change too."

old: "Think of it as everything taking one step into the past and one step away from 'here': *vivo* becomes *vivía*, *mañana* becomes al *día* *siguiente*, and *aquí* becomes *allí*."
new: "Everything moves one step into the past and away from “here”: *vivo* becomes *vivía*, *aquí* becomes *allí* and *mañana* becomes *al día siguiente*, as in *Dijo que vivía allí*."

old: "Combine reported statements, reported questions and perspective changes to reconstruct what happened in a conversation."
new: "You know reported statements from B1 Unit 25 and reported questions from A2 Unit 14. Here you put them together to retell a whole exchange, with a statement and a question in one account, from your own point of view."

old: "When you report a whole exchange, keep the backshift consistent across every clause — if the first verb becomes *había* *visto*, later reported statements in the same account should follow that same shifted timeline."
new: "In one account, keep every verb on the same shifted timeline: if the first verb is *había visto*, the rest follows it, as in *El testigo explicó que había visto al hombre y preguntó si alguien había llamado*."
